what_it_does: Running a large AI language model on a phone requires performing two different kinds of heavy computation: processing your prompt (which involves large matrix multiplications — multiplying huge grids of numbers together — and benefits from the full power of the main processor), and generating each output word one at a time (which involves smaller matrix-vector multiplications that are bottlenecked by how fast the model weights can be read from memory rather than how fast the processor computes). Doing computation inside the memory chip itself — known as processing-in-memory (PIM) — can accelerate the word-generation phase by doing the math where the data already lives, avoiding the slow trip to the processor. The problem is that this requires the model's weight data to be arranged in memory in a specific way (interleaved across banks to match how the PIM units operate), which conflicts with how the main processor prefers the data arranged for the prompt-processing phase, so switching between the two modes normally requires costly data copying. FACIL solves this by adding flexible address-mapping logic to the memory controller — the circuit that translates software memory addresses into physical chip locations — so that different regions of memory can simultaneously use different layout schemes, letting the same weight data satisfy both the PIM units and the main processor without any copying.
